articles.title: Hatterene takes the next examination: Blackthorn at unbeaten Mt. Silver
articles.dek: The Dragons just threw for 368 yards and lost by one. Now they visit a defense allowing 6.8 points per game, with conference position and the Reds’ perfect record at stake.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Blackthorn should arrive at Mt. Silver convinced it can move the ball. The Dragons should also arrive worried about whether moving it will be enough. Hatterene threw for 368 yards and three touchdowns against Sunyshore, and the result was a 21–20 loss. The next opponent has allowed sixty-eight points all season and none over its last two games. That is a useful way to introduce the Game of the Week: an excellent passer trying to make an unbeaten defense spend more of the afternoon answering questions.

Mt. Silver is 10–0. Blackthorn is 8–2. Both currently lead their divisions, and the Reds hold the first seed in the Kanto–Johto table while the Dragons hold the second. A Blackthorn win would bring the records to 10–1 and 9–2, narrowing the separation to one game. A Reds win would make them 11–0 and leave the Dragons 8–3. Those are substantial consequences without pretending this one result settles the postseason. The remaining schedule still has work for everybody.

My pick is Mt. Silver, 27–20. I expect Blackthorn to score and to force a more demanding game than the Reds' recent shutouts. I also expect Connor McLarren's team to have the broader set of answers when the game stops being comfortable. That distinction begins with the defensive matchup, but it does not end there. Mt. Silver has improved its available quarterback play while waiting on injured players, and now it gets a useful runner back.

The most persuasive part of the Eterna win was the absence of ordinary progress. The Thorns gained eighty-four total yards, made three first downs and went zero-for-eight on third down. Tatsugiri completed eight of nineteen for forty-one passing yards. Mt. Silver recorded one sack, so the defensive result cannot be explained simply as a parade of quarterback hits. Eterna repeatedly failed to turn its opportunities into the next set of downs. Blackthorn must make the Reds defend a different kind of possession.

Hatterene is equipped to try. His season line stands at 221 completions in 302 attempts, 2,510 yards, twenty-four touchdowns and four interceptions. Against Sunyshore, he completed twenty-eight of forty-two without an interception. The Dragons reached 385 total yards and sixteen first downs. Those numbers describe a passing attack that can keep several receiving routes relevant, even when the running game has been reduced to an occasional suggestion. They do not describe an offense that needs to begin again from nothing after one loss.

The receiving distribution is where I would start the matchup. Sawsbuck caught six passes for 142 yards against Sunyshore. Exploud caught ten of eleven targets for ninety-four. One supplied the larger gains; the other kept giving Hatterene a productive answer. Mt. Silver has to prevent those jobs from reinforcing each other. If Exploud's catches repeatedly create manageable downs, the defense cannot treat every apparent passing situation as an invitation to chase the quarterback. If Sawsbuck gets behind it, the cost of an otherwise good series changes immediately.

Blackthorn will make that attempt with fewer available receivers. Ninjask, who caught five passes for eighty-nine yards against the Starseekers, is out two weeks. Grovyle remains out five. Together they have contributed 865 receiving yards this season. Their absence is not a reason to declare Hatterene helpless; it is a reason to ask who will take the next useful target and whether that player can make the Reds respect the same space. Sawsbuck and Exploud have just demonstrated they can produce. They should expect an opponent that has noticed.

The running game needs a less ambitious but equally important repair. Blackthorn managed seventeen yards on thirteen attempts against Sunyshore. Furret gained twenty-one on eight carries, while the rest of the rushing line pulled the total backward. The Dragons do not need to imitate a different offense for an entire afternoon. They do need enough successful early-down runs that Hatterene is not repeatedly asked to manufacture the whole possession through the air. An extra four or five useful yards can change how a third down feels.

The final Blackthorn series against Sunyshore explains that need particularly well. Exploud opened with an eleven-yard catch. Furret then lost a yard up the middle. Two incomplete deep passes followed, and Seadra's nine-yard catch on fourth-and-eleven ended two yards short. That was a perfectly ordinary sequence of small failures after a useful opening. Against Mt. Silver, Clair cannot assume the next possession will arrive in time to repair it. Keeping the run from losing ground matters even when the passing total looks excellent.

Mt. Silver's offense has its own questions, but the recent answers have been encouraging. Tic Thorpe followed his three-touchdown passing game at Canalave with four against Eterna. He completed twenty-three of forty for 252 yards, took no sacks and threw no interceptions in the 38–0 win. The Reds converted six of thirteen third downs and gained 352 yards. They did not need every pass to work because the defense kept returning the game to them, and because useful completions became touchdowns in several different hands.

That last point matters with Gregar Jenings still out one week and Josh Alakazam out eleven. Tony Gyarzalez caught six passes for seventy-four yards against Eterna and scored on a thirty-one-yard catch in the third quarter. Plusico Buress had four catches for sixty-eight and a touchdown. The offense has not been reduced to waiting for one missing player to reappear. Thorpe's season passing sample is still much smaller than Hatterene's, so I am not declaring the quarterback question permanently settled. I am recognizing two consecutive productive games in the job.

Garshawn Lynch now has no remaining injury absence. He has 672 rushing yards on eighty-six carries this season, an important available option even before anybody promises a particular workload. Raticate ran for fifty-two yards against Eterna and Vibrava for forty-eight. McLarren has received useful work from the available backs; Lynch's return offers another way to make Blackthorn defend the ground. The Dragons just allowed FLOAT SZN 146 yards, including a seventy-yard touchdown. Their next answer cannot be merely to hope the long run stays off the schedule.

I will watch the first few ordinary rushing possessions more closely than the first spectacular pass. If Mt. Silver keeps gaining enough on the ground to leave Thorpe with manageable decisions, Blackthorn's defense must solve two problems while its offense is missing two receiving contributors. If the Dragons close those runs down, they can make the Reds' passing game demonstrate its new stability under more demanding conditions. A restored runner matters most when the blockers and the situation let him influence the next down.

Blackthorn's route to winning is clear enough to be credible. Give Hatterene usable possession, involve Exploud early, make Sawsbuck's larger opportunities count, and avoid letting the rushing game put the offense behind schedule. On defense, hold the Reds below 120 rushing yards and make Thorpe finish longer series rather than repeatedly work from short fields. My slate also asks the Dragons to convert at least five third downs. Three-for-ten against Sunyshore left too many useful passing yards stranded between scoring chances.

Mt. Silver's route is to keep the game broad. Make the backs contribute, let Tony Gyarzalez and Plusico Buress give Thorpe different receiving answers, and avoid the turnovers that would let Blackthorn skip the difficult part of moving against this defense. My two published keys are to keep the Dragons below twenty-four points and commit no turnovers. Those are measurable targets, not guarantees. They describe the game I expect: Blackthorn occasionally breaking through, then having to build the next score against a team that refuses to donate the opening.

The panel is divided more sharply than my seven-point margin suggests. Rowan, Mara and Ellis have all picked Blackthorn. Dorian and I have Mt. Silver, a temporary alliance that should not be mistaken for agreement about everything he has said this season. I understand the upset case. Hatterene has the production to make even an excellent defense uncomfortable. I am staying with the Reds because the defense is paired with enough current offensive variety to survive that discomfort.

I do not expect another zero beside the visitor's name. Blackthorn has earned more respect than that, and Hatterene's last game supplied specific reasons to give it. I expect the decisive difference to be a possession on which Mt. Silver can still run, still use the tight end and still ask Thorpe for a manageable throw. Blackthorn has just lost by one while making 368 passing yards useful almost everywhere except the final score. My forecast gives the Dragons twenty points and the Reds twenty-seven.

art.alt: Blackthorn’s Hatterene faces Mt. Silver’s Tic Thorpe beneath a silver mountain.

articles.title: The Stone have more than one answer. Mossdeep will make them use every one.
articles.dek: Rustboro returns rested and healthier after a five-touchdown passing game. Tessa Wren examines how the Stone can test the 10–0 Eclipse—and why she still favors Mossdeep.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Rustboro's most useful argument against Mossdeep's unbeaten record is the one it made before the bye. Porygon-Z threw five touchdown passes in a 41–38 win over Cinnabar. The Stone could already ask opponents to respect their runners; that afternoon supplied another answer. Now the 6–4 hosts get My Way, Son back without a remaining injury absence and welcome a 10–0 opponent whose latest receiving performance made almost every available defensive answer look expensive.

My forecast is Mossdeep, 34–24. The Eclipse have sustained more complete offensive production across the season, and their recent passing creates difficult choices for any opponent. Rustboro has a plausible route to changing the result, however. It begins with making that offense wait, continues through using more than one kind of scoring threat, and depends on refusing to let a good Mossdeep receiver turn several normal possessions into a few seconds of pursuit. The Stone need a full afternoon, not one perfect opening drive.

The standings give the game two different kinds of urgency. Mossdeep is first in Hoenn East and holds the leading seed in the Hoenn–Sinnoh conference table. Rustboro is second in Hoenn West, one game behind 7–3 Petalburg and level on record with 6–4 Dewford. Petalburg hosts Sootopolis while Dewford hosts Lavaridge. A Rustboro win could keep the Stone close or bring them level on wins and losses with the Pride, depending on the other result. A defeat could leave a two-game gap if Petalburg wins. None of those possibilities removes Rustboro's own assignment.

Tyler Scarboro has had a bye to prepare for it. The last Stone game is still worth studying because the passing production came through specific, repeatable opportunities rather than a final total alone. Porygon-Z completed sixteen of twenty-five for 268 yards, five touchdowns and one interception. Gibby Timmy caught touchdown passes of thirty-three, ten and forty-six yards. Gengar supplied a nineteen-yard scoring catch. Rustboro made Cinnabar defend several routes to the end zone, and it did so without allowing a sack.

That performance should change how the Eclipse approach the next game. Calling Rustboro a running team is a useful description of its season totals; it is an incomplete description of its last result. The Stone have 1,608 rushing yards through ten games, six more than Mossdeep. They also just showed that concentrating on the ground can leave Porygon-Z with productive receiving opportunities. Michael Dorrill needs a defense that can contest those opportunities without making the returning backfield a secondary concern.

My Way, Son's availability makes that balance more difficult. He has 693 rushing yards on eighty-eight carries this season. Philly has added 504 on 103, and Watchog 202 on thirty-nine. Those are separate contributors rather than a single workload waiting for one injured player to return. Parasect also has no remaining injury absence. The public availability report gives Scarboro more options; it does not tell us exactly how he will distribute them. I want to see whether those options keep Rustboro out of the obvious passing situations Mossdeep would prefer to create.

The Eclipse's defense has earned respect for more than the team's record. Mossdeep has allowed ninety-seven points and 597 rushing yards through ten games, while recording twenty-seven sacks. At Vermilion, Chandelure was sacked five times for thirty-four yards. Joey Sporeter was one of the central defensive contributors in that 45–21 win. Pressure can make a productive passing plan much less comfortable, especially if the run fails to keep the offense on schedule. Rustboro's sack-free afternoon against Cinnabar is evidence of a useful response, not a promise that every opponent will permit it.

There is also an opening the Stone should take seriously. Marshall Flock remains out four weeks. Vermilion completed seventeen of twenty-four passes for 221 yards and three touchdowns without an interception against Mossdeep. The Volts lost heavily because they could not keep up with the Eclipse's offense, but their passing was productive. Scarboro should study that part without assuming the same throws will be available. A good preview distinguishes a demonstrated vulnerability from an automatic instruction for exploiting it.

The other side of the matchup begins with Accel BeckhmJr. Seven catches, 259 yards, four touchdowns. The scoring receptions at Vermilion covered thirteen, sixty, sixty-six and sixty-nine yards. The last three were recorded to the right, and the sixty-six-yard score followed immediately after Vermilion had cut the deficit to ten. That is why a reasonable Rustboro possession plan can disappear quickly: Mossdeep does not always need a long sequence of first downs to undo several minutes of the opponent's work.

The season numbers make it harder to dismiss the performance as an isolated event. Accel has forty-five catches for 1,035 yards and seventeen touchdowns in nine appearances. Dram Marino has completed 176 of 257 throws for 2,640 yards, thirty-one touchdowns and three interceptions. Those totals do not mean the next deep pass must work. They mean Rustboro's defense has to treat the possibility as a recurring part of the assignment, even after it has played several good snaps in a row.

Rustboro's answer cannot stop with Accel, because Gronkaludon caught six passes for seventy yards at Vermilion and has fifty catches for 581 yards this season. Taking away the largest receiving play matters. Leaving an easy succession of smaller completions can still keep the defense on the field and move Mossdeep toward the same scoring opportunity. I would judge the Stone's coverage by whether Marino has to work through genuinely difficult decisions, rather than by whether one famous name has been quiet for a quarter.

Ninjaskamara makes the problem broader again. He ran for ninety-one yards and two touchdowns against Vermilion, scoring from eight and seven yards. For the season he has 1,122 rushing yards and twenty rushing touchdowns, plus fifteen catches for 306 yards and three more scores. Rustboro cannot simply move every available answer toward the deepest receiver and trust the rest to happen behind it. The Eclipse can reach the end zone through a back who has repeatedly finished shorter opportunities as well as a receiver who has made long ones feel brief.

That does not make Mossdeep invulnerable. Marino threw an interception late in the third quarter at Vermilion. The Eclipse finished with thirteen first downs despite 459 total yards, a reminder that this particular win leaned heavily on the largest completions. Rustboro can make the next game less comfortable by preventing those immediate scores and demanding more successful plays in each series. One takeaway would help; building the entire plan around an expected giveaway would be wishful thinking against a quarterback with only three interceptions all season.

The Stone's own defense must also improve on the ending of its Cinnabar win. Rustboro allowed twenty-eight fourth-quarter points, including a ninety-seven-yard kickoff return. Gholdengo finished with 325 passing yards. The offense kept finding another answer, but a ten-point forecast against Mossdeep cannot assume that every defensive failure will be repaid with a touchdown on the next possession. Special teams matter here too. A team trying to keep Marino off the field cannot give away a different kind of rapid score while congratulating itself on the possession count.

My published Rustboro keys are at least 140 rushing yards and fewer than four Mossdeep offensive touchdowns. The first asks the Stone to make their healthier backfield a real part of the contest. The second asks the defense to change the scale of the afternoon. Holding the Eclipse to three offensive touchdowns would not guarantee a win, particularly if kicks or returns become decisive. It would give Rustboro's own passing and running enough space to matter without demanding another forty-one-point performance.

For Mossdeep, the slate asks for at least 350 total yards and no more than one turnover. I expect Marino to find enough receiving work even if Accel does not repeat the extraordinary Vermilion line. Gronkaludon and Ninjaskamara make that forecast less dependent on one player. Defensively, the Eclipse need to make Rustboro earn its passing chances by first resisting the runners. If the Stone can use My Way, Son to produce manageable downs and then find Gibby Timmy beyond them, the game becomes a much more uncomfortable exchange.

Four panelists favor Mossdeep. Dorian has Rustboro winning 38–21, a score that gives him ample room for either a triumphant column or a change of subject. His underlying case is recognizable: the Stone are rested, healthier and coming off a five-touchdown passing game; the Eclipse just conceded three passing touchdowns. My disagreement is about how often Rustboro can make all those advantages work while defending Mossdeep's several scoring threats. The longer season of evidence points me toward the visitors.

I will watch the first ordinary Rustboro third down almost as closely as the first Marino deep throw. If the Stone are facing a manageable distance because the runners have done useful work, Porygon-Z can keep more of his recent answers available. If they are repeatedly trying to recover from lost yards, Mossdeep's pressure can turn the game toward its preferred rhythm. Rustboro has earned a serious preview. Mossdeep has earned the forecast: thirty-four points to twenty-four, with the Stone making the unbeaten visitors use more than one answer.

art.alt: My Way, Son and Accel BeckhmJr face a football field across a stone landscape.
